1.s: God brings charges against Judah: they are like rebellious children, their worship is empty while their hands are full of blood. “Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.”
1.d: “The Holy One of Israel” is Isaiah’s favourite title for God [[tosn:Isaiah 1:4]], used 12 times in chapters 1–39 and 14 times in 40–66 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

2.s: In the last days the mountain of God’s house will be raised up and the nations will stream to it; they will beat their swords into ploughshares. Proud human things will be brought low.
2.d: 2:2–4 is repeated almost exactly in Micah 4:1–3 [[tosn:Isaiah 2:2–4]]. In the New Testament “the last days” begin with the coming of Jesus [[tosn:Isaiah 2:2]] [[bible:Hebrews 1:2]].

3.s: Judgement on Jerusalem’s leaders who crush the poor, and on the proud, adorned women of Zion.
3.d: Judgement on Israel’s leaders continues; removing them would let the mob take over [[tosn:Isaiah 3:1–12]]. “What do you mean that you crush my people, and grind the face of the poor?” [[bible:Isaiah 3:15]].

4.s: After cleansing, “Yahweh’s branch” will be beautiful, and God’s glory will cover Zion like a canopy.
4.d: Some understand “the branch” as the ideal son of David, the Messiah [[tosn:Isaiah 4:2]] [[bible:Jeremiah 23:5]] [[bible:Zechariah 3:8]].

5.s: The Song of the Vineyard: God planted a vineyard, but it yielded wild grapes. He looked for justice, but saw oppression. Woes follow.
5.d: In the Song of the Vineyard God criticises the bad leaders of his vineyard, Israel [[tosn:Isaiah 5:1–7]]. A play on Hebrew words: he looked for justice (mishpat) but saw oppression (mispakh) [[tosn:Isaiah 5:7]]. Compare Jesus’s parable in Matthew 21:33–46 [[tosn:Isaiah 5:1]].

6.s: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, and seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy.” His lips are touched with a coal, and he answers, “Here I am. Send me!”
6.d: Isaiah’s vision of the Lord as King was the turning point of his life [[tosn:Isaiah 6:1–13]]. Jesus used 6:9–10 in his own preaching [[tosn:Isaiah 6:9]] [[bible:Matthew 13:14-15]].

7.s: As Syria and Israel threaten Jerusalem, Isaiah urges King Ahaz to trust God and offers a sign: “The virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”
7.d: The kings of Syria and Israel attacked Judah to force Ahaz to join them [[tosn:Isaiah 7:1–25]]. The Hebrew ‘almah means a young woman of marriageable age; the Greek translators rendered it parthenos, “virgin”, the word Matthew quotes [[tbd:022:Virgin Birth of Jesus]] [[bible:Matthew 1:23]]. The prophecy was fully realised in the birth of Jesus [[tosn:Isaiah 7:14]].

8.s: Isaiah’s son is named Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz, a sign that Assyria will sweep in. Fear God, not conspiracies.
8.d: The stone of stumbling is applied in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8 [[tosn:Isaiah 8:14]]. Hebrews connects 8:17–18 with Jesus [[tosn:Isaiah 8:17]].

9.s: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light… For a child is born to us… His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.”
9.d: God promised that the Messiah would come and rule [[tosn:Isaiah 9:1–7]]. Matthew links the Galilee prophecy with Jesus [[tosn:Isaiah 9:1]] [[bible:Matthew 4:14-16]], and “Mighty God” affirms the Messiah’s divine nature [[tosn:Isaiah 9:6]].

10.s: Woe to unjust lawmakers. Assyria is God’s rod, but its pride will be punished; a remnant will return.
10.d: Judah’s leaders used their power for gain [[tosn:Isaiah 10:1–4]]. The destruction of the Assyrian army in 701 BC fulfilled 10:16, 24–34 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

11.s: A shoot will come from the stump of Jesse, filled with the Spirit; he will judge the poor with justice. The wolf will live with the lamb, and a little child will lead them.
11.d: The new shoot means David’s royal line continues, and Jesus is its final fulfilment [[tosn:Isaiah 11:1]]. The Spirit rests on the Messiah [[tosn:Isaiah 11:2]]. Paul quotes 11:10 [[bible:Romans 15:12]].

12.s: A song of praise: “Behold, God is my salvation. I will trust, and will not be afraid.”
12.d: The prophet’s song of praise closes the reflections on trust in chapters 7–12 [[tosn:Isaiah 12:1–6]]. 12:2 echoes Exodus 15:2 [[bible:Exodus 15:2]].

13.s: An oracle against Babylon: the day of Yahweh will come, and Babylon will be overthrown by the Medes.
13.d: Chapters 13–23 are prophecies against the nations [[tosn:Isaiah 13:1–23:18]]. Babylon fell in 539 BC, but here it also stands for all arrogant nations, like “Babylon the Great” in Revelation [[tosn:Isaiah 13:1]].

14.s: A taunt against the king of Babylon: “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn!”
14.d: “Son of the dawn” is the morning star; the Latin Vulgate has Lucifer, which later Christian tradition made a name for Satan, but the Hebrew text here is about the king of Babylon [[tosn:Isaiah 14:12]].

15.s: A lament over Moab’s destruction: “My heart cries out for Moab.”
15.d: The many Moabite place names show that Isaiah knew Moab well [[tosn:Isaiah 15:1–16:14]]. “My heart cries out for Moab” [[bible:Isaiah 15:5]].

16.s: Moab seeks refuge in Zion; a throne will be established in loving kindness.
16.d: Moab asks Judah for asylum [[tosn:Isaiah 16:1–4]]; oppression will end and a throne will be set up in loving kindness [[tosn:Isaiah 16:4–5]].

17.s: Damascus and Israel will fall; people will look to their Maker.
17.d: Chapters 17–20 announce judgement on Damascus, Israel, Ethiopia and Egypt, starting from the crisis of 734 BC [[tosn:Isaiah 17:1–20:6]].

18.s: A message to Cush (Ethiopia): God watches quietly, and gifts will be brought to him from that distant people.
18.d: Gifts will be brought to the LORD from this distant people [[bible:Isaiah 18:7]].

19.s: Judgement on Egypt, then a stunning promise: “Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”
19.d: Egypt depended on the Nile, and its gods could not save it [[tosn:Isaiah 19:1–10]]. “Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance” [[bible:Isaiah 19:25]].

20.s: Isaiah walks barefoot and stripped for three years as a sign that Egypt and Cush will be led captive by Assyria.
20.d: Sargon captured Ashdod in 711 BC, the occasion of this chapter [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. Isaiah went exposed and barefoot as a sign [[tosn:Isaiah 20:1–5]].

21.s: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon!” A watchman sees the city’s fall. “Watchman, what of the night?”
21.d: John’s prophecy that every Babylon will fall echoes this cry [[tosn:Isaiah 21:9]] [[bible:Revelation 14:8]].

22.s: Jerusalem parties while disaster approaches: “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.” Shebna is replaced by Eliakim, who will hold the key of David’s house.
22.d: The people celebrated the Assyrian retreat of 701 BC without foreseeing Babylon’s attack in 586 BC [[tosn:Isaiah 22:1–4]]. The key of David’s house is applied to Christ in Revelation 3:7 [[tosn:Isaiah 22:22]]. Paul quotes 22:13 [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:32]].

23.s: An oracle against Tyre, the great sea-trading city.
23.d: Tyre was a wealthy seaport whose ties with Judah went back to David and Solomon [[tosn:Isaiah 23:1–18]].

24.s: The whole earth is judged and made desolate because its people broke the everlasting covenant. Then God will reign on Mount Zion.
24.d: The judgements of chapters 13–23 now apply to all creation [[tosn:Isaiah 24:1–23]]. Chapters 24–27 are called the Isaiah Apocalypse because they resemble Revelation [[tosn:Isaiah 24:1–27:13]].

25.s: God prepares a feast for all peoples on his mountain; he will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces.
25.d: The banquet pictures God’s rich provision for all who accept his invitation [[tosn:Isaiah 25:6–8]]. Jesus Christ fulfils the promise to swallow up death [[tosn:Isaiah 25:8]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 15:54]].

26.s: A song of trust: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace.” “Your dead shall live. My dead bodies shall arise.”
26.d: 26:19 most likely refers to the resurrection of the body; the Old Testament says little about it, but this text points ahead to the New Testament [[tosn:Isaiah 26:19]].

27.s: God will slay Leviathan; he sings over his vineyard, and his scattered people will be gathered with a great trumpet.
27.d: Leviathan’s death pictures the end of evil and every power hostile to God [[tosn:Isaiah 27:1]].

28.s: Woe to drunken Ephraim and scoffing Jerusalem. “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone… a precious cornerstone.”
28.d: The first of six woes, contrasting Samaria’s glory with the Lord’s [[tosn:Isaiah 28:1–29]]. The cornerstone is applied to Christ [[tosn:Isaiah 8:14]] [[bible:1 Peter 2:6]].

29.s: Woe to Jerusalem; the people honour God with their lips, but their hearts are far from him. The deaf will hear and the blind see.
29.d: Ariel, another name for Mount Zion, likely means “altar of God” [[tosn:Isaiah 29:1–2]]. Jesus quotes 29:13 [[tosn:Isaiah 29:13]] [[bible:Mark 7:6-7]].

30.s: Woe to those who rely on Egypt: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” God waits to be gracious.
30.d: The fourth of six woes warns Judah not to rely on Egypt [[tosn:Isaiah 30:1–5]].

31.s: Don’t trust Egypt’s horses; God will defend Jerusalem like a lion and like birds hovering over their nest.
31.d: Judah’s talks with Egypt probably took place in 705–701 BC [[tosn:Isaiah 31:1–3]].

32.s: A king will reign in righteousness; the Spirit will be poured out and the wilderness become a fruitful field.
32.d: The king who “shall reign in righteousness” is the Messiah [[tosn:Isaiah 32:1]]. Righteousness brings shalom, peace [[tosn:Isaiah 32:17]].

33.s: God will rise up; the sinners in Zion tremble. The righteous will see the King in his beauty.
33.d: “Yahweh is our judge, Yahweh is our lawgiver, Yahweh is our king” [[bible:Isaiah 33:22]]. A righteous life shows a person truly knows God [[tosn:Isaiah 33:15]].

34.s: God’s judgement on the nations, especially Edom, described in cosmic terms.
34.d: Judgement on the nations on the day of the Lord [[tosn:Isaiah 34:1–17]]. The falling stars are echoed in Revelation 6:13–14 [[tosn:Isaiah 34:4]].

35.s: The desert will blossom like a rose; the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap; the redeemed will return to Zion with singing.
35.d: God will come to change his people, healing the deaf, blind and lame [[tosn:Isaiah 35:1–10]]. Jesus points to such healings [[tosn:Isaiah 35:6]] [[bible:Matthew 11:5]].

36.s: The Assyrian king Sennacherib invades Judah, and his officer mocks Hezekiah’s trust in God.
36.d: Jerusalem’s rescue from Sennacherib is a main event of chapters 1–39 [[tosn:Isaiah 36:1–39:8]]. Chapters 36–39 form a bridge linking chapters 1–35 and 40–66 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

37.s: Hezekiah prays, Isaiah sends God’s answer, and the angel of Yahweh strikes the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib returns home and is murdered.
37.d: Hezekiah’s prayer differs from Ahaz’s reaction decades earlier [[tosn:Isaiah 37:14–20]]. 37:38 mentions Sennacherib’s death, which came in 681 BC [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]]. Assyrian records do not claim Jerusalem was taken [[tbd:008:Hezekiah]].

38.s: Hezekiah falls ill and prays; God adds fifteen years to his life, and the shadow on the sundial goes back. Hezekiah writes a song of thanks.
38.d: Hezekiah’s healing is linked with Jerusalem’s rescue [[tosn:Isaiah 38:1–9]]. His poem has both lament and praise [[tosn:Isaiah 38:9–20]].

39.s: Hezekiah shows his treasures to envoys from Babylon; Isaiah foretells that everything will be carried to Babylon.
39.d: Hezekiah disappointed the Lord by showing off his wealth [[tosn:Isaiah 39:1–8]]. Exile had always been a possibility [[tosn:Isaiah 39:6–7]].

40.s: “Comfort, comfort my people.” A voice cries, “Prepare the way of Yahweh in the wilderness.” All flesh is grass, but God’s word stands forever. Those who wait for God will renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles.
40.d: This chapter introduces chapters 40–66 [[tosn:Isaiah 40:1–31]], in which Isaiah speaks as if the exile had already happened [[tosn:Isaiah 40:1–66:24]]. The Gospels identify the voice in 40:3 as John the Baptist [[tosn:Isaiah 40:3]] [[bible:Mark 1:2-4]].

41.s: God stirs up a conqueror from the east and says to Israel, “Don’t be afraid, for I am with you.” Idols are nothing.
41.d: The Lord calls the nations to trial to show he alone is God [[tosn:Isaiah 41:1–7]]. “Abraham my friend” is echoed in James 2:23 [[tosn:Isaiah 41:8]].

42.s: The first Servant Song: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights.” A bruised reed he will not break.
42.d: The servant here is a royal figure, not the people of Israel [[tosn:Isaiah 42:1–4]]. God used similar words at Jesus’s baptism [[tosn:Isaiah 42:1]] [[bible:Matthew 3:17]], and Matthew applies the passage to Jesus [[bible:Matthew 12:18-21]].

43.s: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.” When you pass through the waters, I will be with you. “Behold, I will do a new thing.”
43.d: God speaks a promise of salvation directly to his people [[tosn:Isaiah 43:1–7]], planning to bring them home from exile [[tosn:Isaiah 43:1]].

44.s: God pours his Spirit on Israel’s children. A satire on idol-making: a man burns half a log for warmth and bows down to the other half. God names Cyrus as his shepherd.
44.d: The promise to pour out the Spirit is linked with restoration [[tosn:Isaiah 44:3]] [[bible:Acts 2:16-18]]. Naming Cyrus is one of Isaiah’s most remarkable prophecies [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]] [[bible:Isaiah 44:28]].

45.s: God calls Cyrus, the Persian king, “his anointed”, to free Israel. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth” Every knee will bow.
45.d: “His anointed”, a title for David or the Messiah, is given to Cyrus, the only foreign ruler to receive it [[tosn:Isaiah 45:1]]. Paul applies “every knee shall bow” to Jesus [[bible:Philippians 2:10]]. The mention of Cyrus is a main reason the book’s unity has been questioned [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

46.s: The idols of Babylon must be carried, but God carries his people from birth to old age.
46.d: A taunt against the self-contradiction of Babylonian religion [[tosn:Isaiah 46:1–2]].

47.s: Proud Babylon, “the mistress of kingdoms”, will sit in the dust.
47.d: Babylon is pictured as a proud queen brought low [[tosn:Isaiah 47:1–4]].

48.s: God refines Israel in the furnace of affliction and calls them to leave Babylon with joy.
48.d: Israel was religious but not truly committed [[tosn:Isaiah 48:1–2]]. The exile was a furnace of suffering [[tosn:Isaiah 48:10]].

49.s: The second Servant Song: the servant will be “a light to the nations”. “Can a woman forget her nursing child?… yet I will not forget you.”
49.d: Traditionally the second of four songs about the suffering servant [[tosn:Isaiah 49:1–13]]. “A light to the nations” is echoed in Luke 2:32 and Acts 13:47 [[tosn:Isaiah 51:4]] [[tosn:Isaiah 42:6]].

50.s: The third Servant Song: the servant gives his back to those who beat him and does not hide his face from shame, trusting God.
50.d: Their sin, not God, caused the exile [[tosn:Isaiah 50:1]]. The suffering servant of 50:4–11 came true in Jesus Christ [[tosn:Isaiah 50:4–11]].

51.s: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness.” Look to Abraham and Sarah. “Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of Yahweh.”
51.d: Each of its three parts begins “Listen to me” [[tosn:Isaiah 51:1–8]].

52.s: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news!” The fourth Servant Song begins: the servant will be exalted, yet his appearance was marred.
52.d: The new rescue from exile will be like the exodus [[tosn:Isaiah 52:4]]. Paul quotes 52:7 about preaching [[bible:Romans 10:15]].

53.s: “He was despised and rejected by men… Surely he has borne our sickness… he was pierced for our transgressions… All we like sheep have gone astray… Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” He is led like a lamb to the slaughter, then sees his offspring.
53.d: The servant had no royal splendour [[tosn:Isaiah 53:2]] and was “a man of suffering” [[tosn:Isaiah 53:3]]; we need not bear God’s punishment because he bore it [[tosn:Isaiah 53:5]]. Philip explains this passage as being about Jesus [[bible:Acts 8:32-35]]. The Servant Songs have ties with chapters 1–6 [[tbd:009:Isaiah, Book of]].

54.s: “Sing, barren, you who didn’t give birth”: Zion will be restored like a wife taken back. “My loving kindness will not depart from you.”
54.d: Jerusalem is like a childless woman who rejoices [[tosn:Isaiah 54:1]] [[bible:Galatians 4:27]]. The promises go beyond the return from exile to the coming of Christ [[tosn:Isaiah 54:1–17]].

55.s: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters!” Buy without money. “My thoughts are not your thoughts.” God’s word will not return empty.
55.d: The last chapter of the comfort prophecies of 40–55 [[tosn:Isaiah 55:1–13]]. The promise to David is fulfilled in Jesus [[tosn:Isaiah 55:3]] [[bible:Acts 13:34]].

56.s: Foreigners and eunuchs who hold fast to God will have a place in his house: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
56.d: The outcasts are invited into God’s redemption [[tosn:Isaiah 56:1–8]]. Jesus quotes 56:7 when clearing the temple [[bible:Mark 11:17]].

57.s: Judgement on idolatry, but God dwells “with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit”.
57.d: Peace “to him who is far off and to him who is near” includes Gentiles and Jews [[tosn:Isaiah 57:19]] [[bible:Ephesians 2:17]].

58.s: True fasting: “to release the bonds of wickedness… to distribute your bread to the hungry” Then your light will break forth like the dawn.
58.d: A charge against self-satisfied religious people [[tosn:Isaiah 58:1–4]], calling them to help those in need [[tosn:Isaiah 58:6–7]] [[bible:Matthew 25:35-36]].

59.s: Your sins have separated you from your God. No one intercedes, so God himself puts on righteousness as armour, and a Redeemer will come to Zion.
59.d: The real problem was that they had not repented [[tosn:Isaiah 59:1–8]]. Paul quotes 59:7–8 [[tosn:Isaiah 59:7–8]], and the Lord as a warrior is echoed in Ephesians 6:14 [[tosn:Isaiah 59:15–17]].

60.s: “Arise, shine; for your light has come.” Nations will come to Zion’s light, kings to the brightness of its rising.
60.d: God will turn Zion’s darkness to light [[tosn:Isaiah 60:1–3]], and the nations will bring gifts, as in Revelation 21:26 [[tosn:Isaiah 60:5–7]].

61.s: “The Lord Yahweh’s Spirit is on me, because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble… to proclaim liberty to the captives… the year of Yahweh’s favor.”
61.d: The servant announces good news that will restore Zion, and Jesus used these words to describe his own mission [[tosn:Isaiah 61:1–3]] [[bible:Luke 4:18-21]].

62.s: For Zion’s sake God will not keep silent until her righteousness shines; she will be called Hephzibah, “Yahweh delights in you”.
62.d: The servant will keep proclaiming good news until Zion’s glory comes [[tosn:Isaiah 62:1–12]]. Zion is renamed “Hephzibah”, “for Yahweh delights in you” [[bible:Isaiah 62:4]].

63.s: A warrior comes from Edom in blood-red garments, having trodden the winepress alone. A prayer remembers God’s mercy in the Exodus: “You, Yahweh, are our Father.”
63.d: Edom’s judgement is an example of how God judges all nations [[tosn:Isaiah 63:1–6]]. The blood-red robes are echoed in Revelation 19:13 [[tosn:Isaiah 63:1]].

64.s: “Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down” “We are the clay, and you our potter.”
64.d: “We are the clay, and you our potter” [[bible:Isaiah 64:8]] [[tosn:Isaiah 64:8]].

65.s: God was found by those who did not seek him. “Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth.” The wolf and lamb will feed together.
65.d: The new heavens and earth will be a place of righteousness [[tosn:Isaiah 65:17]] [[bible:Revelation 21:1]]. Paul quotes 65:1–2 [[bible:Romans 10:20-21]].

66.s: Heaven is God’s throne and earth his footstool; he looks to the humble. Zion gives birth; nations will see God’s glory; new heavens and earth will endure.
66.d: Stephen quoted 66:1–2 in his last sermon [[tosn:Isaiah 66:1]] [[bible:Acts 7:49-50]].
